messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina Chandra had been 31 when her younger brother died suddenly, a death so unexpected that even now she described the memory as “the moment the room split open.” She had been at her apartment in Queens, half-listening to the hum of traffic and editing a story on deadline when her mother called, crying so hard Mina could not make out the words at first. By the time she understood that her brother had been found collapsed on a subway platform and was gone before anyone could help, she was already on the floor, one hand pressed hard against her chest as if she could keep her body from falling apart. What stayed with her was not only the news itself but the feeling that the world had continued moving while her life had stopped. In the days that followed, she kept returning to the last time she had texted him, a casual exchange about nothing important, and she felt engulfed by fear, horror, guilt, and shame, as though she should have somehow known, should have called sooner, should have done something that might have changed the ending. Her divorce had happened the year before, and although she had already been living alone, the loss made the apartment feel harsher and more exposed, every silence louder than the last.

As the weeks passed, Mina found that she could not settle anywhere, even in places she knew were safe. At work in a busy newsroom, where phones rang constantly and colleagues moved past her desk in a blur, she sat rigidly upright, scanning for the slightest shift in tone or an unexpected message on her screen. She was a journalist by trade, accustomed to asking questions and staying alert, but this was different: she felt superalert in a way that never switched off, as if some part of her body was still waiting for another call announcing another irreversible loss. Even at home at night, with the windows locked and the building quiet, she could not relax. She would check the deadbolt, glance toward the hallway, and lie awake with her muscles braced, listening for anything out of place. What frightened her most was how ordinary moments could suddenly feel unsafe. A phone vibrating on the table, a delayed text reply, a pause before someone answered a call — each small interruption seemed to carry the same sharp possibility that had arrived with her mother’s voice. Mina began to feel that if she let her guard down, something terrible would happen again, and that belief kept her tense from morning to night.

The negative feelings did not fade into the background; they stayed close and vivid, coloring nearly everything she did. She felt anger at the unfairness of her brother’s death, guilt for not being there, shame for how often she now wished she could simply stop thinking about him, and fear that her own body would betray her in the same abrupt way. At times, sitting in the newsroom with her laptop open and her coffee cooling beside her, she would suddenly find herself replaying the call, hearing her mother’s voice break again, and her chest would tighten as if the news were happening all over. She had come to believe that calm was no longer trustworthy. Even when there was no immediate danger, her mind stayed on watch, and her body followed suit, unable to lower its guard. Over months, that way of living narrowed her life; she stopped lingering after work, rarely saw friends for dinner, and often left the apartment only when she had to, because being alone in silence left too much room for the fear and shame to rush in. By the time she sought help, Mina was exhausted by her own vigilance. She said she wanted to be able to sleep without checking every sound, to sit at her desk without feeling as if another terrible call might come at any moment, and, more quietly, she feared that if she did not find a way to rest, she would never again feel fully alive.
